Q: Calling a helper function in CodeIgniter emits "Call to undefined method" A:

In your controller, you are using it in the wrong way, it's not a method of the controller so you can't use $this to call it.

A helper can be loaded anywhere within your controller functions (or even within your View files, although that's not a good practice), as long as you load it before you use it. You can load your helpers in your controller constructor so that they become available automatically in any function, or you can load a helper in a specific function that needs it.

To load a helper you can use:

$this->load->helper('name'); // name is the name of the file without extention

Unlike most other systems in CodeIgniter, Helpers are not written in an Object Oriented format. They are simple, procedural functions. Each helper function performs one specific task, with no dependence on other functions.

So, to call a helper function in a controller you should not use:

$this->function_name();

instead use:

function_name();

For example, if you have a helper function in a helper file named custom_helper.php as follows

function myHelper()
{
    // code
}

then you can load it in the controller and call it as follows

$this->load->helper('custom');
myHelper(); // call the function

but it's better to load helpers in the constructor so it'll be available through the whole script.

Update: If your helper file's name is login_helper.php then you can load it in your controller as follows:

$this->load->helper('login');
checkIfLoggedIn($this->session->userdata('loggedIn'));

Read more here.

Q: Any recourse with applying a functional based index to multiple situations? A:

Your index

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX unique_active_order
    ON orders (CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END);

guanrantees there to exist only one active order per customer. Moreover, it will probably only point to rather few rows in the table data, as of all of a customer's orders only one will be open.

A query to get the open orders using the index would have to include CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END and should hence be

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL;

Including tasks for these open orders:

WITH open_orders AS 
(
  SELECT *
  FROM orders
  WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT <whatever subset>
FROM open_orders oo
LEFT OUTER JOIN task t ON t.order_id = oo.id;

Q: Left join multiple columns in three tables A:

I believe you want something like this:

select 
    L.LeaseID AS 'LID', 
    I.Name AS 'Type', 
    L.StartDate AS 'Start', 
    L.EndDate AS 'End', 
    CONCAT(T1.FirstName, ' ', T1.LastName) AS 'Tenant1', 
    CONCAT(T2.FirstName, ' ', T2.LastName) AS 'Tenant2', 
    CONCAT(T3.FirstName, ' ', T3.LastName) AS 'Tenant3', 
    CONCAT(T4.FirstName, ' ', T4.LastName) AS 'Tenant4'
from Leases L
left join Intervals I ON L.Interval = I.Value
left join Tenants T1 ON L.Tenant1 = T1.TenantID
left join Tenants T2 ON L.Tenant2 = T2.TenantID
left join Tenants T3 ON L.Tenant3 = T3.TenantID
left join Tenants T4 ON L.Tenant4 = T4.TenantID

Q: "Transparent" function: perfectly forwarding an argument to the return value A:

The interesting limitation here seems to be lifetime extension rather than reference collapsing itself. std::forward<T>(t) preserves the value category as expected, but once a temporary passes through manipulate(), returning T&& cannot reproduce every lifetime behavior of using the temporary directly.

Q: How StateFlow.collectAsState() works A:

collectAsState() does not automatically call .value every time. Instead, it converts the asynchronous StateFlow into a Compose State<T> object.

When you read .value, Compose registers a snapshot read at that specific point in your Composable. Whenever the underlying MutableStateFlow emits a new list, the State object updates, triggering a recomposition only for the Composables that read that .value.

Detailed Breakdown: How it works under the hood

  1. The Flow Collection: collectAsState() starts a coroutine under the hood to collect emissions from your StateFlow.

  2. The Compose State: Every new emission is pushed into a Compose MutableState<T>.

  3. The Snapshot Read: When your Composable reads .value, Compose notes down that "Component X depends on this state".

  4. The Recomposition: When the ViewModel updates _users.value = newList, the Compose state updates, and Compose instantly re-runs (recomposes) Component X with the new data.

The Problem with your current approach

In your snippet:

kotlin

val users = mainVM.users.collectAsState().value

Use code with caution.

You are assigning the unwrapped value (List<User>) directly to a local variable during recomposition. If you try to use users down the line, Compose might lose track of the state tracking, or you will have to re-read it constantly.

Best Practices & Professional Solutions

To look like a pro, you should use Property Delegation (by) and use the lifecycle-aware compiler extensions.

Option 1: The Idiomatic Compose Way (Using by)

Instead of .value, use Kotlin's by keyword. This automatically delegates the .value getter/setter, making your code clean and readable.

kotlin

// Import these first
import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue

@Composable
fun UserScreen(mainVM: MainViewModel) {
    // 'users' is now directly treated as List<User>
    val users by mainVM.users.collectAsState() 

    LazyColumn {
        items(users) { user ->
            Text(text = user.name)
        }
    }
}

Use code with caution.

Option 2: The Production-Ready Way (Lifecycle Aware)

For production Android apps, collecting flows using collectAsState() can waste resources when the app goes into the background. The industry standard is to use collectAsStateWithLifecycle().

Add this dependency to your build.gradle.kts:

kotlin

implementation("androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose:2.8.0") // Use the latest version

Use code with caution.

Update your Composable:

kotlin

import androidx.lifecycle.compose.collectAsStateWithLifecycle
import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue

@Composable
fun UserScreen(mainVM: MainViewModel) {
    // This safely stops collecting when the app is in the background
    val users by mainVM.users.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() 

    UserList(users)
}

Use code with caution.

Summary for your mental model

  • StateFlow = The pipeline delivering the data from the ViewModel.

  • collectAsState() = The bridge turning the pipeline into a Compose-readable state tracker.

  • by keyword = The syntactic sugar that removes the need to type .value everywhere.
